headline: A 2023 law renews and expands federal programs to fight human trafficking, support victims, and require more research and reporting on the problem.
what_it_does: The law makes the U.S. Advisory Council on Human Trafficking permanent and reauthorizes grants and programs that help trafficking victims. It creates new grants and a pilot program for youth at risk of being trafficked, and it changes the definition of child abuse so that any child identified as a trafficking victim counts. It also requires several government reports and studies, and it includes some statements of what Congress believes agencies and companies should do.

who_it_affects.group: Victims of human trafficking in the United States
who_it_affects.how: Federal health, justice, and labor programs that provide benefits and services to citizen and lawful permanent resident victims are reauthorized through fiscal year 2028.

who_it_affects.group: Children and youth at risk of trafficking
who_it_affects.how: A new pilot program will fund community-based organizations in underserved areas that support young people at risk of being trafficked.
Children involved in both the child welfare and juvenile justice systems may benefit from competitive grants that help states coordinate their services.

who_it_affects.group: Children in foster care who go missing or are abducted
who_it_affects.how: State child welfare agencies must keep regular contact with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and law enforcement and share information such as photos and risk factors to help recover them.

State foster care and adoption plans must include the new information-sharing requirements for missing or abducted children, and a child identified as a trafficking victim is now treated as a victim of child abuse and neglect.

who_it_affects.group: Federal employees and executive branch officers
who_it_affects.how: They must meet minimum standards on human trafficking, including a ban on engaging in trafficking while employed by the federal government, and agencies are encouraged to add trafficking training.

who_it_affects.group: Large companies doing business in the United States
who_it_affects.how: Companies with 500 or more employees are encouraged, though not required, to adopt a written policy against trafficking.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection receives authorized funding through fiscal year 2028 to enforce the ban on imports made with forced labor.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted January 5, 2023. Many grant and program authorizations run through fiscal year 2028, and some reports and studies have their own deadlines. Several provisions are statements of congressional opinion rather than binding rules.
